title: I don't think I understand roofs and I desperately need help...

And I finally figured out what's wrong and I don't... quite understand what the correct fix is? So I have a bunch of the nice SF_Outside_A3 roofs, I've kinda got a little frankensteined version of some of my favorites I've just been experimenting with here, mostly Avery's lovely reworks but a couple others I like (this is mostly just for practice though). So they don't have tops and sides? So... how are you supposed to use these A3 roofs? Are there really only like 3 usable roofs available? I'm so confused and I feel like I'm missing something key but tutorials I'm finding on building and such only uses the like 3 basic roofs, and don't seem to touch on these at all so I'm so very confused.

posts.author: TeiRaven
posts.body:
I don't think you're missing anything--the RTP, autotile-based roofs (these square ones) are really, really bland. Any time you see interesting roofs, it's because someone put in the time to make extra pieces and import them into their project! I don't remember all of the creators who have made them, but I know Avery has some--and I think Candacis has others? I'm not as up on my MZ resources as I am on my XP ones. Have a look in the
MZ Resources Section
, I think you'll like what you find!
Having said that though, "interesting" roof pieces can still be a little tricky to use (to line up correctly on the tileset, to figure out which piece goes where to get a convincing shape, etc). Avery has some spectacular tutorials that should help you get underway! I don't have the direct links immediately to hand, but I think
this thread has all of her tutorials
, and I know for sure she has some that involve how to make and how to use custom roofs.
I hope that gets you going in the direction you want to go!

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
The point of those roofs on the A tab is they represent the angled roofs that you typically see on houses. You're looking at one side of the angle and you don't see the other because it's...on the other side.
The other roofs are beveled at the edge then flat in the middle, which is more like what you typically see on businesses or other large buildings.
You can certainly do whatever you like with making different shapes with them, and some people only use the C tab roofs for everything, but that's what the intent is.

posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
Additionally, we can't tell if you were using the tiles wrong because you didn't show any of your maps.
because there is one thing where people have gone wrong in the past, and that is the number of tiles per floor.
That is something you have to decide for yourself, but it should either be two tiles or three tiles per floor - while it is possible to do maps with a single tile per floor scale, that rarely works put for new users.
and the roof should then be of the same height unless you are going for a specific effect.
so if you make a house of two tiles wall height, use a roof of also two tiles height above that.
and then, as said above go to the B-E decoration and place things like chimneys and windows to break up the monotony of the walls and roofs.

posts.author: TeiRaven
posts.body:
Okay, I think I see what's giving you trouble in a few places! The pictures help immensely. I know the first two are not intended to be totally functional houses, they're meant for experimentation, but I'd like to tell you what I see and maybe some of it will help you in your quest!
For the first one (white with a grey roof), you have a whole tile worth of eaves. I think you'll like it better if you make yourself some tiles that are only a portion of that width (I'd start with about a quarter, and go up from there) for the left and right edges. That way, you can have overhanging eaves, but they'll be a little more in proportion with the building. With the windows, were you aiming for skylights or dormers? Dormers are usually also done with an B/C/D/E tileset piece, and have a little bit of shading of their own to show that they stick out at a different angle.
I think what you're seeing on the second one (white with wood shingles) is that the house feels like it has no depth. In order to stack a second story on top of the first one, the roof would need to extend backwards some (probably with an additional, partial-square tile), or it looks like the bottom floor is paper-thin--and again, the eaves are very big in comparison to the rest of the house, so try making a narrower tile to be the edges of this one too!
For the third house (brick with the grey roof), I think it's the second story that's throwing you. For a house this shape to work, you'll probably need a custom roof tile to be the spot where all the roof angles come together. I'm blanking on what that part of/style of roof is called (I know there's a word for it) but what you're seeing (or not seeing!) is that the peaks of those roofs should come together in a + shape somewhere, and the south-facing section should probably have a triangular peak rather than a flat edge facing down. The deck is a fantastic touch, I really like that!
Finally, the last house (brick with the blue roof) looks nice to me! It has more depth than the earlier white house, for reasons I can't quite articulate but I think have to do with the shadows on the side looking more natural. The thing my eye hangs up on is the dark line across where the south wing sticks out, and that the windows on that wing and up on the second floor are really up close next to the eaves. If you haven't explored the possibilities of shift-mapping (right clicking to select a specific part of an autotiled area, then holding Shift and clicking to use that particular tile in a particular place) I highly recommend it as your next thing to try!
I hope something in all of that is helpful to you! I personally find autotile roofs actually really difficult to use (especially without adding my own extra eaves and dormers and such) so good on you for all the experimenting you've done! Keep at it!

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
I'd suggest you read up on shift-click mapping and practice that a bit - it will help some of these designs to not see borders on the walls or roofs that are clearly going into the ground or showing the tip of a roof.
Your T-shape is very weird because it doesn't seem to respect the perspective that the tiles are drawn in. The only way you would see walls, two stories of roof, then more wall, is if that fourth story was literally built on top of the roof below it. Houses aren't made that way.
I'm genuinely unsure as to what kind of construction you're trying to show there, but for any kind of shapes like that I think you're better off with the C tab roofs.
The autotile roofs aren't great for emulating large, deep buildings because they're one side of an angled roof - they only look like they get higher, not like they go back.
And then you can add more stories or whatever to that.

posts.author: Kenen
posts.body:
In addition to the great advice above, I'd suggest looking at some reference images from games that the tilesets are based off of. This will help give you a point of reference for how the base materials are intended to be used.
Obviously, much more can be done with the material, but if you look at these images, you should see some immediate similarities between them and the basic roof tiles included with the editor.

posts.author: LindyGraham
posts.body:
HyperMushrambo,
Grain of salt, as I don't know your background or what preparation/research you have already accomplished...
I find it helpful when sorting out my buildings rather than solely doing a brute force trial and error, is to sort out exactly what I imagine them a head of time. Knowing the style terminology then allows for an expedited image search for exactly what I am trying to emulate/accomplish. These searches then allow for excellent reference materials if I need to add anything custom alterations to my tile sheets. It also lets me search the forums efficiently for advice on those styles if it has already been mentioned. If it hasn't been mentioned, knowing the terms for what I am looking to achieve as an end product greatly helps those that wish to grant aid with a response to my posts.
- Not saying you have done anything wrong. Merely elaborating on what I have found helpful for myself that possibly could be of aid to others. None the less, looking at a variety of examples should always facilitate the probability of further creativity in the future.
